description: Test your knowledge of PA H3 | Microcytic Anemias — iron distribution, recycling, and absorption mechanisms essential for diagnosing and treating iron deficiency anaemia.

cards.text: Name the three functional pools of iron in the body and identify which contains the largest amount.
cards.answer: 1) Functional pool (~65–70%): haemoglobin in RBCs (~2500 mg), myoglobin, haem enzymes. 2) Storage pool (~20–25%): ferritin (~800–1200 mg) and hemosiderin. 3) Transport pool (<0.1%): transferrin-bound iron (~3–4 mg). The functional pool dominates.

tip.tip: F-S-T: Functional > Storage > Transport. Remember: haemoglobin is the biggest iron consumer.

cards.text: Why is the body almost entirely dependent on iron recycling rather than dietary absorption?
cards.answer: 25 mg of iron is recycled daily from senescent RBC destruction by splenic macrophages, while dietary absorption adds only 1–2 mg/day. The recycling rate is ~12–25× greater than absorption, so loss of efficient recycling causes iron deficiency faster than malabsorption alone.

tip.tip: 25 mg recycle vs 1–2 mg absorbed — recycling dominates. Spleen is the iron recycler.

cards.text: Compare haem iron and non-haem iron absorption. Which is more efficient and why is non-haem more clinically important?
cards.answer: Haem iron: 20–30% absorption, minimally affected by enhancers/inhibitors, uses HCP1 transporter. Non-haem iron: 1–8% absorption, highly affected by enhancers/inhibitors, uses Dcytb and DMT1. Non-haem is clinically important because it comprises 85–90% of dietary iron.

tip.tip: Haem is efficient but rare (10–15% diet). Non-haem is inefficient but abundant (85–90%) — this is where iron deficiency starts.

cards.text: Describe the non-haem iron absorption pathway from the duodenal lumen to portal blood.
cards.answer: Gastric acid reduces Fe³⁺ in lumen → Dcytb (ferrireductase) reduces Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ → DMT1 transporter moves Fe²⁺ into enterocyte → iron stored as ferritin or exported → Ferroportin (FPN1) on basolateral membrane exports Fe²⁺ → Hephaestin oxidises Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ for transferrin loading.

tip.tip: Dcytb (reduce), DMT1 (import), Ferroportin (export). Hephaestin oxidises before transferrin binding.

cards.text: Why are patients on proton pump inhibitors at risk for iron deficiency anaemia?
cards.answer: PPIs reduce gastric acid, which prevents Fe³⁺ solubilisation in the duodenal lumen. Without adequate acidity, the non-haem iron reduction step (Dcytb) is impaired, and iron absorption drops significantly. This is an iatrogenic cause of iron deficiency.

tip.tip: No acid → no Fe³⁺ solubilisation → impaired Dcytb reduction → iron deficiency. PPI = risk factor.

cards.text: What is the single physiological mechanism by which the body excretes excess iron?
cards.answer: The body cannot excrete iron — it has no iron excretion pathway. Iron loss occurs only through blood loss, desquamation (skin shedding), or menstruation. Therefore, the duodenal absorption gate is the only regulatory mechanism available.

tip.tip: Zero excretion. Absorption is the only control point. This is why iron overload (haemochromatosis) is dangerous — no dump valve.

cards.text: Why does prescribing vitamin C alongside iron tablets enhance absorption of non-haem iron?
cards.answer: Vitamin C reduces Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ in the duodenal lumen, keeping iron soluble and available for DMT1 transport. It mimics the role of gastric acid and enhances the first committed step of non-haem iron absorption.

tip.tip: Vitamin C = additional reducing agent (like gastric acid). More Fe²⁺ ready for DMT1 = better absorption.

cards.text: Ferroportin (FPN1) is the only iron exporter in the body. Which membrane surface does it occupy and what happens to iron after it exits the enterocyte?
cards.answer: Ferroportin occupies the basolateral membrane of the enterocyte. After iron exits, hephaestin (a copper-dependent ferroxidase) oxidises Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, and the iron is immediately bound to transferrin for transport in portal blood to the bone marrow and storage sites.

tip.tip: Ferroportin on basolateral side = gateway to blood. Hephaestin = oxidation step before transferrin binding.
